justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a gradual upward drift from a baseline near 63, which likely represented the prevailing level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 63.3 is essentially anchored to the current value with only minimal expected movement, consistent with the idea that short-term price or index levels tend to mean-revert or drift slowly absent a major catalyst. At the one-week horizon, I projected a modest increase to 63.8, reflecting a slight positive trend assumption while acknowledging that a week is still a relatively short window. The one-month estimate of 64.5 extends that gentle upward trajectory further, implying a slow secular drift rather than any sharp directional move.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 1.8 units on either side, reflecting the relatively constrained range of outcomes possible within a single trading session or day. By one week, the interval widens to roughly ±3.8 units, capturing the greater variability that can accumulate across multiple sessions. At one month, the interval expands to ±7.5 units, acknowledging that over four or so weeks, macroeconomic data releases, policy decisions, and shifting sentiment can move things substantially in either direction. The increasing width is a straightforward reflection of volatility compounding with the square root of time.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected adverse macro shock — such as a surprise contraction in key economic data, a geopolitical escalation, or a sudden tightening in financial conditions — could easily drive the variable well below 61.5 even within a day or two. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst such as better-than-expected economic data, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty could push values above 72 within the month.

The one-month interval in particular deserves scrutiny, because 30 days is long enough for regime changes in sentiment or fundamentals to materialize. If there is a scheduled major event — a central bank decision, an earnings season, or a geopolitical negotiation — during that window, tail outcomes become meaningfully more probable than the 5% implied by the interval boundaries. My intervals assume roughly normal background conditions; any structural break or fat-tail event would invalidate that assumption and could easily produce outcomes in the tails or beyond them.
